nodes.name: Quadriceps
nodes.layer: — (§1.2: a parent, neither drawn nor selectable; the TypeScript value follows the platform lane, the forearm's groups use 'mixed')
nodes.layerEvidence: Its four muscles span the surface (rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis) and the deep layer (vastus intermedius) (radiopaedia.quadriceps_muscles, kenhub.quadriceps_femoris); 'mixed' is the honest value if the type needs one.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Three of its four muscles reach the surface and the vastus intermedius is deep (radiopaedia.quadriceps_muscles, kenhub.quadriceps_femoris); the forearm marks its mixed-layer groups 'partial'.
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: The canonical list (shared/capabilityRank.ts) holds rectus_femoris, vastus_lateralis, vastus_medialis and vastus_intermedius separately, not the group.
nodes.location: Front of the thigh and its inner and outer sides, from the hip to the kneecap, in a surface layer over a deep one.
nodes.whatItDoes: Straightens your knee. The rectus femoris, one of its four muscles, also helps bend your hip.
nodes.shapeNote: Together these muscles make up most of the front of the thigh, so they may shape most of its contour, mostly through the three at the surface. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: A group, not a muscle: work is counted for the four muscles inside it.
Many people have an extra head between or beside the vasti; the atlas counts the four usual muscles.

nodes.name: Rectus femoris
nodes.layerEvidence: Superficial among the quadriceps (radiopaedia.quadriceps_muscles); the vastus intermedius lies deep to it (kenhub.quadriceps_femoris).
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: The superficial quadriceps muscle at the front of the thigh, over the vastus intermedius (radiopaedia.quadriceps_muscles, kenhub.quadriceps_femoris).
nodes.location: Front of the thigh, at the surface, from the front of the pelvis just above the hip joint to the kneecap.
nodes.whatItDoes: Straightens your knee and bends your hip. It is the only quadriceps muscle that crosses the hip.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute to the contour down the front of the thigh, over the vastus intermedius. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: It crosses both the hip and the knee: in one study it was less active in a leg press than in knee extension, and less active when effort to straighten the hip was added, and the authors tied the difference to whether the exercise also straightens the hip. That is short-term muscle activity, not growth.

References differ on how much it does at the hip: some say it helps bend the hip, and a cadaver study estimated from muscle size and leverage that it could give most of the hip-bending force with the hip straight or bent up to about 60 degrees.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, thigh:thigh.rectus_femoris.function, is reviewed.

nodes.name: Vastus lateralis
nodes.layerEvidence: On the outer side of the femur among the quadriceps (statpearls.vastus_lateralis, radiopaedia.quadriceps_muscles); the iliotibial band, a sheet of fascia, lies over its lower outer part (kenhub.iliotibial_tract). Kenhub adds that the tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus cover its outer side (Q20, uncited summary line).
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: The largest quadriceps muscle, on the outer side of the front of the thigh; what lies over it lower down is fascia (the iliotibial band), not muscle (statpearls.vastus_lateralis, kenhub.iliotibial_tract).
nodes.location: Outer side of the front of the thigh, at the surface, from the top of the thigh bone to the outer edge of the kneecap; the largest of the four quadriceps muscles.
nodes.whatItDoes: Straightens your knee and helps keep the kneecap steady. It does not act on the hip.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute to the outer contour of the thigh. Lower down, the iliotibial band, a thick band of fascia, lies over its outer side. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Studies of changes to how the leg is placed have not separated its work from the vastus medialis; the atlas does not split their work.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, thigh:thigh.vastus_lateralis.function, is reviewed.

nodes.name: Vastus medialis
nodes.layerEvidence: On the inner side among the quadriceps (radiopaedia.quadriceps_muscles); its lowest fibres form a bulge above the inner kneecap, and the sartorius crosses over its upper part (kenhub.quadriceps_femoris). Surface for its lower part, which is where §1.2's layer holds; the upper part is crossed by the sartorius (a note, not a deviation).
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Its lower fibres form a noticeable bulge above the inner side of the kneecap, but the sartorius crosses over its upper part (kenhub.quadriceps_femoris).
nodes.location: Inner side of the front of the thigh, from the inner side of the thigh bone to the inner edge of the kneecap; at the surface in its lower part, where the sartorius does not cross it.
nodes.whatItDoes: Straightens your knee and helps keep the kneecap steady; its lowest fibres pull on the inner edge of the kneecap.
nodes.shapeNote: Its lowest fibres form the bulge above the inner side of the kneecap, so it may contribute to the inner contour of the thigh just above the knee. Higher up the sartorius crosses over it. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Its lowest fibres run more nearly across than the rest and are often called the vastus medialis oblique (VMO); whether they form a separate part is not settled.
Studies of changes to how the leg is placed have not separated the work of its lower fibres from the vastus lateralis; the atlas does not split their work.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, thigh:thigh.vastus_medialis.function, is reviewed.

nodes.name: Vastus intermedius
nodes.layerEvidence: Deep to the rectus femoris and completely surrounded by the other quadriceps muscles (kenhub.quadriceps_femoris; radiopaedia.quadriceps_muscles 'vastus intermedius deep'); no surface outcrop, as §1.2 has it.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Completely surrounded by the other quadriceps muscles, under the rectus femoris (kenhub.quadriceps_femoris).
nodes.location: Front and outer side of the thigh bone, deepest layer, under the rectus femoris and between the other two vasti.
nodes.whatItDoes: Straightens your knee. It does not act on the hip.
nodes.shapeNote: Deep under the rectus femoris and surrounded by the other quadriceps muscles, so it has little or no contour of its own; it may add to the general thickness of the front of the thigh. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: It cannot be tested on its own: the quadriceps muscles are tested together.
Some people have an extra muscle head beside it, the tensor of the vastus intermedius.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, thigh:thigh.vastus_intermedius.function, is reviewed.

nodes.layerEvidence: Its members span the surface (long head of the biceps femoris, semitendinosus), a middle layer (semimembranosus, under the semitendinosus) and a deeper one (short head, under the long head) (kenhub.biceps_femoris, kenhub.semimembranosus, elsevier.semitendinosus); 'mixed' is the honest value if the type needs one.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Two members are near the surface for most of their length and two lie under them (kenhub.biceps_femoris, kenhub.semimembranosus); the forearm marks its mixed-layer groups 'partial'.
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: The canonical list holds biceps_femoris_long_head, biceps_femoris_short_head, semitendinosus and semimembranosus separately, not the group.
nodes.location: Back of the thigh, mostly from the sitting bone at the bottom of the pelvis to the top of the two lower-leg bones just below the knee; the biceps femoris on the outer side, the semitendinosus and semimembranosus on the inner side.
nodes.whatItDoes: Straightens your hip and bends your knee; all of its parts except the short head of the biceps femoris cross both joints.
nodes.shapeNote: Together these muscles make up most of the back of the thigh, so they may shape most of its contour, mostly through the long head of the biceps femoris and the semitendinosus at the surface. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: A group, not a muscle: work is counted for the four parts inside it.
Some references count only the three muscles that cross the hip as hamstrings and leave out the short head of the biceps femoris; it is listed here because it bends the knee with them.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, thigh:thigh.hamstrings.function, is reviewed. The references describe the group as such, so the parent has a function claim; it has no node actions.

nodes.name: Biceps femoris, long head
nodes.layerEvidence: Runs superficially in the back and outer thigh under skin, fat and fascia for most of its length, covered by the gluteus maximus at its upper end (kenhub.biceps_femoris); the short head lies deep to it (kenhub.biceps_femoris).
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: At the surface for most of its length, but covered by the gluteus maximus at its upper end (kenhub.biceps_femoris); lower down it shares the outer edge with the short head.
nodes.location: Back of the thigh on the outer side, at the surface, from the sitting bone to the head of the fibula just below the outer side of the knee; the gluteus maximus covers its upper end.
nodes.whatItDoes: Straightens your hip and bends your knee; with the knee bent it also turns the lower leg outward.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute to the outer side of the back of the thigh, and with the short head it forms the upper outer border of the hollow behind the knee. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Some studies found its activity higher relative to the inner hamstrings in some hip-extension exercises, such as a 45-degree hip extension, than in knee-bending ones such as the Nordic or a leg curl; a bent-knee bridge was an exception. That is short-term muscle activity, not growth.
Its turning of the lower leg and the thigh outward is not counted as a separate action here.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, thigh:thigh.biceps_femoris_long.function, is reviewed.

nodes.name: Biceps femoris, short head
nodes.layerEvidence: One head lies deep to the other (kenhub.biceps_femoris); no excerpt, in the first pass or the second review (R31, R32), names which, so the short head as the deeper rests on its origin on the lower back of the thigh bone (R32) and on §1.2. Near the knee it lies along the outer edge of the long head's tendon (koreamed.biceps_femoris_short_head) and helps form the upper outer border of the popliteal fossa (statpearls.popliteal_region), whose roof is fascia and skin (teachmeanatomy.popliteal_fossa): a possible small surface window that §1.2 does not have (deviation D1). The second review found no source describing the short head as visible there (R14).
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Under the long head for most of its length, by inference (kenhub.biceps_femoris says one head lies deep to the other; R32 gives the short head's origin on the lower thigh bone); the small part beside the long head's tendon near the knee is not a separately visible outline.
nodes.location: Back of the thigh on the outer side, under the long head, from the back of the thigh bone above the knee to the head of the fibula.
nodes.whatItDoes: Bends your knee and, with the knee bent, turns the lower leg outward. It does not cross the hip, so it does not straighten the hip.
nodes.shapeNote: Lies under the long head, so it has little or no contour of its own; near the knee it may add to the outer edge of the hollow behind the knee. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: It is the one part of the hamstrings that does not cross the hip; imaging studies give a mixed picture of how much different hamstring exercises use it. That is short-term muscle activity, not growth.
Some references do not count it as a hamstring because it does not cross the hip.
Its turning of the lower leg outward is not counted as a separate action here.

nodes.name: Semitendinosus
nodes.layerEvidence: Posterior to (over) the semimembranosus and inner to the long head of the biceps femoris (elsevier.semitendinosus); the semimembranosus lies deep to it (kenhub.semimembranosus).
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: At the surface on the inner side of the back of the thigh (elsevier.semitendinosus), but its lower part is a long, round tendon, so its belly shows only in the upper part.
nodes.location: Back of the thigh on the inner side, at the surface, from the sitting bone to the inner side of the top of the shin bone; it ends in a long, round tendon.
nodes.whatItDoes: Straightens your hip and bends your knee; it also turns the lower leg inward.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute to the inner side of the back of the thigh; near the knee it is mostly tendon, and a visible tendon is not muscle size. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Imaging studies found it among the most used hamstrings in knee-bending exercises such as the Nordic and leg curls. That is short-term muscle activity, not growth.
Its turning of the lower leg and the thigh inward is not counted as a separate action here.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, thigh:thigh.semitendinosus.function, is reviewed.

nodes.name: Semimembranosus
nodes.layerEvidence: Deep to the semitendinosus and superficial to the adductor magnus (kenhub.semimembranosus): the middle layer. The outcrop rests on inference: near the knee it forms the upper inner border of the popliteal fossa (teachmeanatomy.popliteal_fossa lists it alone; kenhub.popliteal_fossa with the semitendinosus), and the fossa's roof is only fascia and skin. No source says it is visible, and Kenhub places it deep to the semitendinosus 'along its entirety' (deviation D2). The second review's own search for a part showing beside the semitendinosus (R13) found no citable source either.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Covered by the semitendinosus for most of its length (kenhub.semimembranosus); near the knee it forms the upper inner border of the hollow behind the knee under only fascia and skin (teachmeanatomy.popliteal_fossa).
nodes.location: Back of the thigh on the inner side, under the semitendinosus, from the sitting bone to the inner knuckle of the shin bone just below the knee.
nodes.whatItDoes: Straightens your hip and bends your knee; with the knee partly bent it also turns the lower leg inward.
nodes.shapeNote: Mostly covered by the semitendinosus; near the knee it forms the upper inner border of the hollow behind the knee and may contribute to the inner side of the back of the thigh there, though one reference places it under the semitendinosus along its whole length. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: In one small study of a hip-extension exercise it was among the most active hamstrings. That is short-term muscle activity, not growth.
It cannot be tested on its own: the muscles of the back of the thigh are tested together.
Its turning of the lower leg and the thigh inward is not counted as a separate action here.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, thigh:thigh.semimembranosus.function, is reviewed.

nodes.name: Sartorius
nodes.layerEvidence: A superficial muscle crossing the front of the thigh at a slant, in front of the quadriceps (radiopaedia.sartorius).
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: At the surface along its whole course (radiopaedia.sartorius), but it crosses over the quadriceps toward the inner knee, so its own outline shows mostly as a line between its neighbours (an inference from its course).
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: Exists in the canonical list (shared/capabilityRank.ts, mapped there to hip_flexors); the node is adjacent and has no catalog key in §1.2.
nodes.location: Front of the thigh, at the surface: the longest muscle in the body, running at a slant from the front of the hip bone on the outer side to the inner side of the top of the shin bone.
nodes.whatItDoes: Helps bend your knee and your hip, and helps move the thigh out to the side and turn it outward, as when sitting cross-legged.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute to the line that runs across the front of the thigh from the outer hip toward the inner knee; its inner edge forms the outer border of the hollow just below the groin. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Shown beside the thigh muscles because of where it sits; thigh specialization does not target it.
References differ on how much it does at the hip: some list hip bending among its main actions, others say it assists.
None of its actions is strong on its own; one reference says it mostly works together with other muscles.

claims.statement: The quadriceps femoris is a group of four muscles at the front of the thigh: the rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis and vastus intermedius. Anatomy references describe it as the main muscle group that straightens the knee, through the quadriceps tendon to the kneecap and on to the top of the shin bone, and as helping keep the kneecap steady. Of the four, only the rectus femoris crosses the hip, where it also helps bend the hip.

claims.statement: The textbook quadriceps has four heads, but many people have more. A 2025 review pooling 18 cadaver studies (1,066 limbs) found a five-headed form in just over half of the limbs and the classic four-headed form in fewer than half; the extra head was most often a head of the vastus lateralis, and an independent tensor of the vastus intermedius was found in a minority. In a cadaver study of 41 limbs from a South Indian population, an extra head lay between the vastus lateralis and the vastus intermedius in a little under half.

claims.statement: The rectus femoris straightens the knee with the other three quadriceps muscles and bends the hip. It is the only quadriceps muscle that crosses the hip: it arises from the front of the pelvis just above the hip joint (the anterior inferior iliac spine and the rim above the hip socket) and joins the other quadriceps muscles in their common tendon (the patellar tendon). References differ on how much it does at the hip. Some say it helps or assists in bending the hip; a cadaver study of 22 limbs estimated from the muscles' size and leverage, as a theoretical share rather than a measured force, that from a straight hip to about 60 degrees of bending it could give roughly two thirds of the hip-bending force, the iliopsoas's share rising sharply beyond that, and counted both among the main hip flexors.

The authors concluded that its activity in multi-joint exercise is low and does not rise with fatigue, unlike the vasti, and that these differences depend on whether the exercise also asks the hip to straighten. That is short-term muscle activity, not growth.

claims.statement: The vastus medialis straightens the knee through the quadriceps tendon and helps steady the kneecap through fibres that attach directly to it. Its lowest fibres, often called the vastus medialis oblique (VMO), run from the inner side of the lower thigh bone to the upper inner edge of the kneecap and are described as an inner stabiliser of the kneecap. Whether they form a separate part of the muscle is not settled: a systematic review of 26 studies found a change in fibre direction between the upper and lower parts in most, but too little good-quality evidence to say the muscle divides in two.

sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q1, Q4; generated summaries with index markers into the statpearls.com copy, article 32250). sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Abdomen and Pelvis, Rectus Femoris Muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q3, Q77). Extends the leg at the knee with the other quadriceps and helps flex the hip with the sartorius and iliopsoas; two heads, from the anterior inferior iliac spine and the acetabular ridge; joins the other quadriceps in the patellar tendon. Q77 gave the authors as Murdock CJ, Mudreac A and Agyeman K (13 Nov 2023) and a PubMed id 30969719 seen only in a PubMed 'reviews' link, not confirmed; no Bookshelf id was found, so the statpearls.com URL is used. sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Bony Pelvis and Lower Limb: Vastus Lateralis Muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q6): Biondi and Varacallo, updated August 2023. Introduction and structure visible: the largest quadriceps component, positioned on the outer side of the femur; origin on the intertrochanteric line, greater trochanter, linea aspera, gluteal tuberosity and lateral intermuscular septum; insertion through the quadriceps tendon to the outer kneecap and, through the patellar tendon, the tibial tuberosity. The summary's function lines ('a primary extender of the knee', 'stabilizes the knee joint' with the vastus medialis) drew on these excerpts and other references without saying which line came from which; the rest was behind a subscription wall.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Bony Pelvis and Lower Limb, Hamstring Muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q2): the hamstrings are the biceps femoris (long and short heads), semitendinosus and semimembranosus; the group contributes strongly to hip extension and knee flexion; most cross both joints; the short head starts on the femur and crosses only the knee, and some authors question whether it is a true hamstring. Authors and update date not shown in this lane's results; full text not seen.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Bony Pelvis and Lower Limb: Posterior Thigh Muscles
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q5; the summary named NBK542215 and an August 2023 update). Members of the hamstrings; except the short head of the biceps femoris they cross the hip and the knee, from the back of the pelvis to the top of the tibia and fibula; the long head, semitendinosus and semimembranosus arise from the ischial tuberosity, the short head from the linea aspera; the biceps femoris crosses the knee on the outer side and the other two on the inner side. The summary's line on open and closed kinetic chains was attributed to a sibling article (ID 32248) and is not used. Authors not shown; the rest was behind a paywall. Second review (R30): no search showed this article's Bookshelf id; the statpearls.com copy is point-of-care 32252 (updated 21 Aug 2023), and a mirror of a PubMed link carried id 31194372 for a StatPearls record of this title, not confirmed. NBK542215 rests on the first pass's Q5 alone.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Bony Pelvis and Lower Limb: Thigh Sartorius Muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q8): Walters and Varacallo, updated 28 Aug 2023; a PubMed record (30422484) carries this title. The Bookshelf id NBK532889 was seen only in a mirror URL, not on an NCBI page. Partial text only.

sources.title: Kenhub: Quadriceps femoris muscle: Anatomy, innervation, function
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q16, Q20). Function: the primary function is to extend the leg at the knee; the rectus femoris, crossing both joints, also helps with thigh flexion. Relations: the vastus intermedius lies deep to the rectus femoris and is completely surrounded by the other quadriceps muscles; the sartorius crosses the superficial surface of the vastus medialis; the lowest vastus medialis fibres lie almost horizontal and form a noticeable bulge above the inner kneecap; the vastus lateralis is the largest, lies superficial to the biceps femoris and its outer side is covered by the tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus; synonyms of the vastus medialis include 'vastus internus' and 'teardrop muscle'. Author and update date not shown; the summary noted Kenhub's phrasing differs a little between versions.

sources.title: Kenhub: Posterior thigh muscles - Hamstrings
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q17, a summary across four Kenhub pages): the hamstrings' primary role is bending the knee and moving the thigh backward at the hip. Lines specific to one muscle are filed under that muscle's Kenhub key. Author and date not shown.

sources.title: Kenhub: Biceps femoris: Origin, insertion, innervation, function
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q17, Q18, Q50, Q68): two heads, one deep to the other; the long head from the ischial tuberosity, the short head from the linea aspera and supracondylar line, both to the head of the fibula; at the hip it extends the thigh and turns it outward, at the knee it flexes the leg and turns it outward when the knee is partly bent; only the long head crosses the hip; for most of its length it runs superficially in the back and outer thigh under skin, fat and fascia, covered at its upper end by the gluteus maximus. Author and date not shown. Second review (R32, restricted to kenhub.com): the short head arises quite distally from the long head, on the lower third of the linea aspera; R32 did not show the Relations section, and no excerpt in either pass names which head lies deep to the other.

sources.title: Kenhub: Semimembranosus: Origin, insertion, action, innervation
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q11, Q17, Q21): actions thigh extension and internal rotation at the hip, leg flexion and internal rotation at the knee; with the feet planted it extends the hip and helps raise the trunk; deep to the semitendinosus, superficial to the adductor magnus and inner to the biceps femoris 'along its entirety'; its upper part is covered by the gluteus maximus. Author and date not shown. Second review (R13, R20): no source found describing a part of the semimembranosus visible beside the semitendinosus; R20 confirmed its origin and actions.

sources.title: Kenhub: Semitendinosus: Origin, insertion, innervation, action
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q10, Q17): Action: hip joint, thigh extension, thigh internal rotation, stabilizes pelvis; knee joint, leg flexion, leg internal rotation; with the trunk upright it turns the thigh inward, with the trunk bent forward it extends the thigh. Author and date not shown.

sources.title: Kenhub: Sartorius muscle: Anatomy, attachments, function

Q19 did not show its actions; Q55's summary listed them from Kenhub and anatomy.net together, so no action is cited to this key.

sources.title: Kenhub: Iliotibial tract (IT band): Anatomy, origin, insertion

A second Kenhub page (fasciae of the hip and thigh) added that it blends with the vastus lateralis aponeurosis lower down; that line is not used. Author and date not shown.

sources.title: Kenhub: Popliteal fossa: Anatomy and contents

sources.title: Radiopaedia: Sartorius muscle

Authors and revision date not shown. Second review (R15, R16, the second restricted to radiopaedia.org): the action section lists hip and knee flexion as primary, lateral rotation and weak abduction as secondary, and says 'None of these actions are strong in isolation - most of its action is synergistic.'

The result was a changeset page of this article (radiopaedia.org/articles/vastus-medialis-muscle/changesets/147140/edits); the article URL is given here.

sources.title: TeachMeAnatomy: Muscles of the Anterior Thigh
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q52). The summary drew on this page and the TeachMeAnatomy encyclopaedia entries for the quadriceps, rectus femoris, vastus intermedius and sartorius together: the quadriceps' primary action is knee extension, the rectus femoris also helps flex the hip and is the only one of the group to cross both joints; the vastus intermedius arises from the front and outer femoral shaft, extends the knee and helps steady the patella; the sartorius flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the thigh at the hip and flexes the knee. Which line came from which of these pages was not shown; they are kept under this key.

sources.title: TeachMeAnatomy: Muscles of the Posterior Thigh - Hamstrings
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q24; the summary drew on this page and the encyclopaedia entries for each muscle): the hamstrings primarily extend the thigh at the hip and flex the leg at the knee; the biceps femoris is the most lateral, its main actions knee flexion and outward rotation of the knee, with a weaker role in extending and outwardly rotating the thigh; the semitendinosus flexes the knee, extends the hip and turns the thigh and leg inward; the semimembranosus lies deep to the semitendinosus, arises higher on the ischial tuberosity and turns the thigh and leg inward; tibial division for the long heads, common fibular division for the short head.

sources.title: TeachMeAnatomy: The Popliteal Fossa

sources.title: IMAIOS e-Anatomy: Rectus femoris muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q53, the page's summary fields through the imaios.cn mirror): actions knee extension and hip flexion; femoral nerve; insertion on the patella and, through the patellar ligament, the tibial tuberosity.

sources.title: IMAIOS e-Anatomy: Vastus lateralis muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q54, through the imaios.cn mirror): extends and stabilises the knee; a pure knee extensor, unlike the rectus femoris; joins the other quadriceps in the quadriceps tendon to the base and outer border of the patella.

sources.title: Kumazaki et al., Action and Contribution of the Iliopsoas and Rectus Femoris as Hip Flexor Agonists Examined with Anatomical Analysis (Juntendo Medical Journal, 2022)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q31, Q34): 22 formalin-fixed limbs (10 male, 12 female adult Japanese cadavers); moment arms and physiological cross-sectional areas used to estimate maximal torque; the rectus femoris gave roughly two thirds of the estimated flexion torque from a straight hip to about 60 degrees, the iliopsoas rising sharply beyond; the iliopsoas the faster, the rectus femoris the more powerful flexor; the iliopsoas and rectus femoris are the main agonists, the sartorius and adductor longus synergists. Estimates from cadaver morphometry, not measurements in living people. Co-authors and PubMed id not shown. Second review (R12): agrees with every figure used, and adds the authors' own caveat that their method does not estimate actual torque or speed, only maximal and relative contributions on a theoretical basis; the claim now says so.

sources.title: Ema, Sakaguchi, Akagi and Kawakami, Unique activation of the quadriceps femoris during single- and multi-joint exercises (European Journal of Applied Physiology 116:1031-1041, 2016)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q37, Q40): surface EMG of the rectus femoris, vastus lateralis and vastus medialis in knee extension and leg press, and with added isometric hip-extension effort; rectus femoris activity higher in knee extension than in leg press, the vasti unchanged; added hip-extension effort lowered rectus femoris activity; rectus femoris activity in multi-joint exercise low and not rising with fatigue, unlike the vasti. Volume and pages from a library catalogue record; DOI from the Springer link. Sample size and PubMed id not shown (a PubMed id tried in Q62 belonged to another record). Second review (R1): three experiments, 11 adults (added hip-extension effort), 15 men (knee extension against leg press) and 14 men (leg press to exhaustion); the authors add that the differences between muscles and exercises depend on whether hip-extension torque is exerted.

sources.title: Miyamoto, Wakahara and Kawakami, Task-Dependent Inhomogeneous Muscle Activities within the Bi-Articular Human Rectus Femoris Muscle (PLoS One, 2012)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q35, Q60): surface EMG from the lower, middle and upper regions of the rectus femoris during maximal isometric knee extension and hip flexion; hip flexion gave lower EMG than knee extension in every region; the regions did not differ in knee extension; in hip flexion the lower region was lower than the middle and upper regions. Published 27 March 2012. Sample size and PubMed id not shown (a PubMed id proposed in the query, 22479583, was not confirmed). Second review (R2): agrees with every finding used; sample size still not shown.

sources.title: Smith, Dixon, Bowyer, Stephenson, Chester and Donell, Can vastus medialis oblique be preferentially activated? A systematic review of electromyographic studies (Physiotherapy Theory and Practice 25(2):69-98, 2009)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q45, Q80): 20 papers, 387 participants; altering lower-limb joint orientation or adding a co-contraction did not preferentially enhance vastus medialis oblique activity over the vastus lateralis; significant methodological limitations in the evidence. Abstract only. Second review (R3): confirmed as Physiotherapy Theory and Practice 2009 Feb;25(2):69-98, a review of English-language EMG studies to February 2008; author order beyond Smith not confirmed.

sources.title: Smith, Nichols, Harle and Donell, Do the vastus medialis obliquus and vastus medialis longus really exist? A systematic review (Clinical Anatomy 22(2):183-199, 2009)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q7, Q66): 26 papers, 699 healthy knees and 591 specimens with patellofemoral dysfunction; most showed a substantial change in fibre alignment between the upper and lower parts of the muscle; one or two nerve branches; a separating fascial plane in a small proportion; insufficient good-quality evidence to say whether the muscle divides into an upper and a lower part. Abstract only; DOI not shown.

sources.title: Piagkou, Triantafyllou, Georgiev, Tsakotos, Olewnik, Landfald and Gonera, Systematic Review and Prevalence Meta-Analysis of Quadriceps Femoris Morphology: Significance of the Quadriceps Tendon in Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction (Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology 10(3):250, 2025)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q36, Q64; also on PMC as PMC12286201): 18 cadaver studies, 1,066 limbs; a five-headed quadriceps the most common configuration, the classic four-headed form next; among accessory heads the vastus lateralis type the most frequent; an independent tensor of the vastus intermedius in a minority of limbs. The pooled figures came from an abstract excerpt in Q36; Q64 did not return them. Methods and confidence intervals not seen. Second review (R10, R29): published 30 June 2025; R29 returned the same pooled figures from the abstract (54.11 and 40.74 for the five- and four-headed forms, 21.35 for the vastus lateralis type, 13.54 for an independent tensor of the vastus intermedius), so they no longer rest on one excerpt.

sources.title: Sam et al., Prevalence of the additional head of quadriceps femoris in the South Indian population: a cadaveric and radiological study (Scientific Reports 11:16132, 2021)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q33, Q65): 41 formalin-fixed cadaveric limbs and 88 MRI scans; an additional head in a little under half of the cadaveric limbs, always between the vastus lateralis and the vastus intermedius. The abstract was seen through a university repository copy; co-authors, DOI and the MRI figure not shown. Second review (R11): Scientific Reports 11, article 16132 (August 2021), DOI 10.1038/s41598-021-95374-z, from Christian Medical College, Vellore; 41 limbs from 22 male and 19 female cadavers aged 30 to 70; the extra head consistently between the vastus lateralis and vastus intermedius. The MRI figure still not seen.

sources.title: Bourne, Williams, Opar, Al Najjar, Kerr and Shield, Impact of exercise selection on hamstring muscle activation (British Journal of Sports Medicine 51(13):1021-1028, 2017)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q38, Q41): 24 recreationally active men; part 1, surface EMG ratios of the outer (biceps femoris) to inner hamstrings in 10 exercises: eccentrically highest in the 45-degree hip extension, lowest in the Nordic and the bent-knee bridge; concentrically highest in the lunge and 45-degree hip extension, lowest in the leg curl and bent-knee bridge; part 2, muscle functional MRI: a higher long head to semitendinosus ratio after the 45-degree hip extension than after the Nordic; after hip extension, T2 rose more in the long head, semitendinosus and semimembranosus than in the short head; after the Nordic, the semitendinosus rose most. Abstract only. Second review (R4): agrees; after the Nordic the semitendinosus rose more than the other hamstrings (p 0.002 or less). A follow-up in six women (Messer et al. 2018) found the same direction and is not cited.

sources.title: Ono, Higashihara and Fukubayashi, Hamstring Functions During Hip-Extension Exercise Assessed With Electromyography and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (Research in Sports Medicine 19(1), 2011)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q39, Q63, Q79): six men, five sets of ten hip-extension repetitions; EMG of the long head of the biceps femoris and the semimembranosus higher than the semitendinosus; only the semimembranosus showed a significant rise in T2 and cross-sectional area immediately after; the authors concluded the long head and semimembranosus were selectively recruited. No publisher page was found; the URL is the Waseda University researcher database page that lists the paper. Pages given as 42-52 there and 1-11 in a conference abstract; DOI and PubMed id not confirmed. Second review (R5): agrees; a later study cites it as surface-EMG work, which the claims no longer need to say. A conference abstract of the same group adds a gracilis arm and is not cited.

sources.title: Fernandez-Gonzalo, Tesch et al., Individual muscle use in hamstring exercises by soccer players assessed using functional MRI (International Journal of Sports Medicine 37(7):559-564, 2016)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q70): 36 professional soccer players in four groups (Nordic hamstring, flywheel leg curl, Russian belt, conic pulley); muscle functional MRI; the flywheel leg curl gave the largest hamstring and gracilis use; the Nordic mainly affected the gracilis, semitendinosus and short head of the biceps femoris; no single exercise increased T2 in every hamstring and synergist measured. The PubMed id came from an aggregator page; the journal year was listed as 2017 with an April 2016 epub. Co-authors and DOI not shown; abstract only. Second review (R7): the flywheel leg curl gave the largest rises (gracilis, semitendinosus, short head, then long head) and the Nordic smaller ones in the same three; the Russian belt and conic pulley only slight rises in the semitendinosus and long head. sources.title: Mendiguchia et al., Nonuniform changes in MRI measurements of the thigh muscles after two hamstring strengthening exercises (Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research 27(3):574-581, 2013)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q71): 11 male professional soccer players, one leg doing eccentric leg curls and the other lunges (three sets of six); MRI before and 48 hours after; no significant change in the semimembranosus or the short head of the biceps femoris; changes along most of the semitendinosus and at one level of the long head and adductor magnus; leg curls load all regions of the semitendinosus, lunges mainly the upper long head and adductor magnus. Seen through the Edith Cowan University repository record; co-authors and PubMed id not shown; abstract only. Second review (R8): agrees, including no significant change for the semimembranosus and short head; the abstract does not tie that line to one exercise, so the claims say only that no change was found after the session. A PubMed link 23443215 appeared without a title (not confirmed as this record), and a conference poster from the same line reported a different pattern; neither is used.

sources.title: Hirose, Kagaya and Tsuruike, The task dependent differences in electromyography activity of hamstring muscles during leg curls and hip extensions (PLOS ONE, 2021)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q72, Q73): 20 men; isometric leg curls and hip extensions at two knee angles, at a submaximal and a maximal effort, hip neutral; surface EMG from the upper and lower regions of the long head of the biceps femoris and the semitendinosus; the long head to semitendinosus ratio was higher in hip extension with the knee straight than in a leg curl at 90 degrees, and differed by task in the upper region but not the lower. PubMed id not shown. Second review (R6): the long head to semitendinosus ratio near the hip was higher in straight-knee hip extension than in a leg curl at 90 degrees, but did not differ from a leg curl at 30 degrees; the claim now says so.

sources.title: Maeo, Huang, Wu, Sakurai, Kusagawa, Sugiyama, Kanehisa and Isaka, Greater Hamstrings Muscle Hypertrophy but Similar Damage Protection after Training at Long versus Short Muscle Lengths (Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise 53(4):825-837, 2021)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q43, Q75): 20 untrained adults (13 men, 7 women), seated leg curls with one leg and lying leg curls with the other, 12 weeks, MRI muscle volume; larger gains on the seated side for the whole hamstrings and each muscle that crosses the hip, no difference for the short head of the biceps femoris; a second, eccentric phase found similar damage protection. Q75's figures came from secondary summaries, Q43's from a summary with the PubMed link; DOI not shown; abstract only. Second review (R9): agrees; the abstract names the 'monoarticular hamstring muscle', which is the short head of the biceps femoris, and a secondary summary names the short head.

sources.title: Park et al., needle EMG approach to the biceps femoris short head, medial or lateral, a cadaver study (Annals of Rehabilitation Medicine 45(1):42-48, 2021)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q50) and in this lane's continuation on 20 Oct (Q81, Q82): 21 dissected lower limbs; in the lower thigh the short head lies lateral to (along the outer edge of) the long head's tendon, with the common fibular nerve along the tendon's inner edge; the authors judged a lateral needle approach safer and a site near the upper apex of the popliteal fossa more accurate. The exact title is 'Which Approach Is Most Optimal for Needle Electromyographic Examination of the Biceps Femoris Short Head: Medial or Lateral?'; the title here is shortened to keep the word 'optimal', which is not a growth claim here, out of the copy, as the forearm's S4 title was reworded. Volume, pages and DOI from Q81; co-authors and PubMed id not shown. Abstract only; a needle-placement study, cited for location only.

sources.title: Larsen et al., The effects of hip flexion angle on quadriceps femoris muscle hypertrophy in the leg extension exercise (Journal of Sports Sciences 43(2):210-221, 2025)
sources.notes: Added by the second review; checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (R22, R25, R28): 22 untrained men, ten weeks, two sessions a week, leg extensions with one leg at about 40 degrees and the other at about 90 degrees of hip flexion, the side allocated at random; muscle thickness by ultrasound, not MRI; the authors report 'extreme' evidence for a larger rectus femoris response at 40 degrees and 'strong' evidence of no difference for the vastus lateralis. The acute imaging study it builds on (Mitsuya et al. 2023) was seen only in secondary write-ups (R28) and is not cited.

deviations.fixedIn10: Biceps femoris, short head: kind head, target, layer 'deep', no outcrop
deviations.evidence: Kenhub: 'this muscle consists of two heads, one lying deep to the other' (kenhub.biceps_femoris, Q50), which supports 'deep' only by inference, since it does not say which head (the second review found no excerpt that does, R31, R32). But a cadaver study of 21 limbs places the short head 'along the lateral margin of the long head's tendon in the distal thigh' (koreamed.biceps_femoris_short_head, Q50; 'The short head was found to sit lateral to the long head tendon', Q81), StatPearls lists 'the biceps femoris muscle (short and long heads)' as the upper outer border of the popliteal fossa (statpearls.popliteal_region, Q56), and the fossa's roof is 'popliteal fascia and skin' (teachmeanatomy.popliteal_fossa, Q56).
deviations.assessment: Not a contradiction of the layer: the belly is deep. It suggests a small surface window just above the outer back of the knee, beside the long head's tendon, which §1.2 does not list. Whether it can hold a 44 px exclusive square on a 360-wide canvas is for the drawing lane to measure.
deviations.proposal: Keep §1.2's layer. The drawing lane may add a Back-surface outcrop of the short head beside the long-head tendon above the knee if it fits a 44 px square; otherwise the short head stays on Back-deep only and the shape note already says it has little or no contour of its own. The adversarial review decides; this lane does not change §1.2.

deviations.fixedIn10: Semimembranosus: intermediate layer with a surface outcrop beside the semitendinosus
deviations.evidence: The middle layer is supported: 'Semimembranosus is deep to semitendinosus, superficial to adductor magnus and medial to biceps femoris along its entirety' (kenhub.semimembranosus, Q21). The outcrop rests on inference only: TeachMeAnatomy lists the semimembranosus alone as the upper inner border of the popliteal fossa and Kenhub lists it with the semitendinosus (Q56), and the fossa's roof is fascia and skin (Q56). No source states that the semimembranosus shows at the surface, and Kenhub's 'along its entirety' could be read against any outcrop. A line calling it 'the most medially located muscle in the posterior compartment' came only from anatomy.net and anatomy.app (Q61), outside the evidence standard's list, and is not cited.
deviations.assessment: A weakly supported outcrop, not a contradicted one: the inference places it near the knee at the upper inner border of the hollow behind the knee, beside the semitendinosus tendon, not along the length of the thigh.
deviations.proposal: Keep §1.2. The drawing lane places the outcrop low on the inner back of the thigh, above the knee, and the diagram note says it rests on the popliteal-fossa border rather than on a source that shows it visible. A human anatomy review should confirm it.

deviations.fixedIn10: The short head's parent is the hamstrings
deviations.evidence: Elsevier: 'The term "hamstrings" is the collective name given to the long head of biceps femoris, semitendinosus, and semimembranosus muscles' (elsevier.semitendinosus, Q26); StatPearls: 'The article notes some authors therefore question whether it is a true hamstring' (statpearls.hamstring, Q2). StatPearls, Radiopaedia, Kenhub and TeachMeAnatomy all list the short head with the hamstrings.
deviations.assessment: A grouping choice, not an anatomical error: the short head is a posterior thigh muscle that bends the knee with the hamstrings. Recorded so the review sees the wording.
deviations.proposal: No change. The hamstrings' function claim and the short head's caveats say that some references leave it out.

singleSourceFunctionClaims: None. Every function claim cites four to seven references.

Sentences inside function claims that rest on one reference: thigh.rectus_femoris.function, the cadaver estimate of its share of hip-bending force (juntendo.hip_flexor_agonists); thigh.vastus_medialis.function, the review of whether the oblique fibres are a separate part (pmid.19090000) and the oblique fibres as an inner kneecap stabiliser (radiopaedia.vastus_medialis); thigh.vastus_intermedius.function, 'helps steady the kneecap' (teachmeanatomy.anterior_thigh, said as 'one reference adds'); thigh.biceps_femoris_long.function, its hip role as weaker than its knee role (teachmeanatomy.hamstrings, said as 'one teaching reference'); thigh.semimembranosus.function, its pull at the hip as weaker than the biceps femoris's (radiopaedia.semimembranosus, said as 'one reference'); thigh.sartorius.function, the cadaver study's 'synergist' (juntendo.hip_flexor_agonists). Each is worded as one reference's finding. disagreementsAndWording: Rectus femoris at the hip. StatPearls ('helps flex the hip') and Elsevier ('assists') word hip flexion as help; Kenhub, TeachMeAnatomy, Loyola, IMAIOS and Radiopaedia list it as one of its two actions; a cadaver morphometry study estimated it gives roughly two thirds of the hip-flexion torque up to about 60 degrees and named it one of the two main agonists. The claim says the references differ; the node action is prime on the cadaver estimate and the action lists.

Sartorius at the hip. Radiopaedia lists hip flexion among its primary actions; Elsevier says it assists, and the cadaver study names it a synergist. The claim says the references differ; the node action takes the weaker reading (assist), as the forearm does for helpers.

Hamstrings at the hip. TeachMeAnatomy calls the biceps femoris's hip role weaker than its knee role, and a Radiopaedia line calls the semimembranosus's hip extension weaker than the biceps femoris's. Elsevier, Kenhub and Loyola list hip extension for each, StatPearls says the group contributes strongly to hip extension, and two EMG and imaging studies found the long head and semimembranosus selectively recruited in hip-extension exercises. Each weaker-role line is said in its claim as one reference's view; the node actions stay prime.

Short head of the biceps femoris as a hamstring: Elsevier's semitendinosus page names only the three hip-crossing muscles as 'hamstrings' and StatPearls notes some authors question it; StatPearls, Radiopaedia, Kenhub and TeachMeAnatomy list it with the hamstrings. Said in the group claim and the short head's caveats (deviation D3).

The vastus medialis oblique: Radiopaedia describes the oblique fibres as a component and an inner kneecap stabiliser; a systematic review found too little good-quality evidence to say the muscle divides in two. The function claim says both; the node stays one muscle, as §1.2 has it.

Hamstring imaging findings conflict for the short head and the semimembranosus: after hip extension their MRI signal rose by different amounts in one study, while another found no significant change in either after leg curls or lunges. The selectivity claims say each finding and call the picture mixed rather than choosing one.

Rotation at the knee and hip by the hamstrings and the sartorius is position-dependent and secondary in every source; it is said in the claims, never counted (no knee-rotation action exists; hip rotation is not a thigh region action).

Sartorius at the knee (second review). Every reference lists knee flexion, Elsevier without qualification and Radiopaedia among its primary actions, but Radiopaedia also says none of its actions is strong in isolation and most of its action is synergistic (R16). The claim now says so, and the knee.flexion row is assist, like its hip-flexion row.

Which head of the biceps femoris is deeper (second review). Kenhub says one head lies deep to the other without naming it, and no excerpt in either pass names it (Q50, R31, R32). The short head as the deeper rests on its origin on the lower back of the thigh bone and on §1.2's layer; the appearance claims now word it as that inference.
productQuestions: Rectus femoris hip.flexion is prime on the evidence. If the review prefers StatPearls' and Elsevier's 'helps' and makes it assist, two things follow: §1.2's external rule for the hips' listing of the rectus femoris (a prime mover of one of the listing region's actions) no longer holds, and the thigh's region action hip.flexion has no prime own target (the sartorius, its only other own performer, is adjacent and assist).
